title: Wait before pleasure
hookLine: when a pleasure beckons, pause, and picture both the enjoying and the regret after (Enchiridion 34)

lines: THE OPEN FRIDGE, THE LAST SLICE.
HALF A SECOND BEFORE THE HAND MOVES.
cards: The kitchen is dark except for the open fridge, and the last slice of cake is right there. Or it's the tab with the shopping cart, or the one more episode button counting down from ten.
There's a moment, maybe half a second long, between the urge showing up and your hand moving. It's easy to miss entirely.
Section thirty-four of the Enchiridion lives inside that half second, and asks you to stretch it out.

teach.h: LET THE PLEASURE WAIT FOR YOU.
teach.b: When the impression of some pleasure arrives, Epictetus says, be careful not to be swept off by it. Let the thing wait for you. Give yourself a little delay.
He doesn't say refuse. He says wait. In the delay, call to mind two times.

teach.h: PICTURE THE ENJOYING, AND THE REGRET.
teach.b: The time when you'll be enjoying the pleasure. And the time after, when you've had it, and you're sorry, and you're scolding yourself. Both are real.

teach.h: PICTURE THE GLADNESS OF HOLDING OFF.
teach.b: Then set a third picture against them: how glad you'll be, and how well you'll think of yourself, if you hold off. Three scenes, and you get to watch all of them before you choose. And the honest ending.
If, after all that, it seems the right time to enjoy the thing, Epictetus allows it.

teach.h: IF YOU TAKE IT, DON'T BE CARRIED.
teach.b: Just take care, he says, that its sweetness and its pull don't overpower you, and remember how much better it is to know you've won that small contest. This isn't a rule against pleasure.
It's a rule against being carried.
The pleasure that survives the wait is one you've chosen.

how: Some people practicing Stoicism put a short delay between an urge and acting on it, and in that pause picture both the enjoyment and how they'll feel afterward.

o: the pleasure itself, and the regret that can follow it
a before and after photo of a habit you broke
the good side and the bad side of a person

games.q: wait before pleasure — tap the pairs.
p: let the pleasure wait for you
don't let its pull carry you

s: he says wait. if it's the right time, enjoy it, without being carried.
he asks you to picture the regret afterward, not just the enjoying
both times, and then the gladness of holding off.

games.q: the urge arrives: one more episode, and it's midnight. what does Epictetus say to do first?
o: give in quickly, so it stops bothering you.
let it wait, and picture both the enjoying and the after.
games.why: a delay, and two pictures. then, if it's still the right time, you choose it, instead of being carried.

practice: Think of an urge you know well, a snack, a scroll, a purchase, a drink, a reply typed too fast, and picture it arriving.

Run the three pictures slowly: the enjoying, the after and how you might feel, and the gladness of having waited. You don't need to decide anything now; just practice watching all three before your hand moves.

wordCard.voice: Two pictures, Epictetus says to call to mind before giving in: the moment of the pleasure, and the moment after, sorry and self-scolding. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: wait. Half a second can grow into a real choice. See you tomorrow.
